planting.note: Mount unpotted on bark, wire, or driftwood in very bright, indirect light with strong airflow; Houston is a vigorous grower that quickly outgrows both of its parent species and clumps into offset colonies within a couple of seasons.

directions: Houston was hybridized by botanist Mark Dimmitt in the 1980s by crossing Tillandsia stricta with Tillandsia recurvifolia, producing a rosette larger and more vigorous than either species alone. The narrow, silver-scaled leaves shade from bright lime green at the base to soft silvery-gray toward the tips, and a tall, pale pink bloom spike opens into violet-blue flowers over several weeks. It shares a hybrid grex with the related cultivar 'Cotton Candy' but carries firmer, more upright foliage and a taller inflorescence than its softer-leaved sibling. Soak or mist thoroughly two to three times a week, then shake out trapped water and let the foliage dry fully within a few hours to prevent basal rot.

planting.note: Grow in a large hanging basket or elevated container with a coarse, fast-draining bark mix; this is a big-growing Aechmea, and offsets are usually left to develop into full-size rosettes over a year or more before being separated.

directions: Burgundy is an old hybrid raised by pioneering bromeliad breeder Mulford Foster by crossing Aechmea distichantha var. schlumbergeri with Aechmea weilbachii var. leodiensis, and it has remained in cultivation for decades on the strength of its foliage alone. Broad, arching leaves flush a deep wine-red to burgundy across the whole rosette, intensifying with brighter light rather than staying green like many Aechmea species. A tall, branched inflorescence eventually rises above the leaves, carrying small flowers over pink-flushed bracts typical of its distichantha parentage. Keep the central cup filled with water, feed the roots lightly since Aechmea take up most nutrients through the tank, and expect a large, long-lived rosette that produces just a few big pups rather than many small ones.

planting.note: Best grown in a hanging basket or elevated pot rather than as flat groundcover, since Donger sends its pups out on distinctly elongated stems that need room to arch away from the mother rosette; use only filtered or rain water in the cup, as chlorinated tap water can scorch the variegated margins.

directions: Donger arose as a naturally variegated sport of the popular dwarf hybrid Neoregelia 'Fireball', discovered in a Princeton, Florida shadehouse and later patented for its distinct look. Unlike plain Fireball's solid green-margined leaves, Donger's narrow rosette carries dark maroon leaves edged in white that shifts to pink and then to vivid rose in strong light. Small pale blue flowers appear low in the central cup in late fall and again in winter, but the plant is grown almost entirely for its two-tone foliage. Give it the same bright, filtered light and shallow, fast-draining planting as its Fireball parent, and expect offsets on noticeably longer stolons that make it well suited to baskets and elevated displays.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden — Neoregelia 'Donger' plant profile
Florida Council of Bromeliad Societies — Neoregelia cultivar guide
